criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly attributes the flat, launch-time gap to training-serving skew (and/or leaky offline evaluation) rather than drift, and accurately describes the mechanisms — dual computation paths diverging on edge cases, point-in-time/leakage or staleness on txn_count_24h, and the missing-value distribution mismatch on merchant_avg_ticket — with no technical errors. Deduct for calling it drift, for claiming retraining on recent data fixes it, or for garbling point-in-time correctness.

Full marks: covers all four stages — diagnosis (skew vs drift), root-cause confirmation, fix, and prevention — and addresses both named features plus the shared code-path issue. Partial credit if one stage (typically confirmation or prevention/monitoring) or one of the two features is omitted.

Full marks: justifies WHY a flat-from-launch signature implies skew not drift, WHY future-peeking or a complete-table backfill inflates offline metrics, and WHY 30% default imputation concentrates error — and ties each proposed fix to the specific mechanism it addresses. Partial credit for correct conclusions asserted without the underlying reasoning.

Full marks: an organized diagnose -> confirm -> fix -> prevent narrative usable in a design review, using precise vocabulary (point-in-time correctness, feature store, feature logging, PSI/KS, as-of join). Deduct for a disorganized list of buzzwords or vague, unattributed claims.

expected_answer_points: Correctly diagnoses this as training-serving skew (and/or a leaky offline eval), NOT data drift, justified by the signature: a flat gap present from launch versus the gradual temporal decline that would indicate drift.

Identifies the dual-code-path mechanism — nightly Spark/SQL for training vs online Python/Redis for serving — producing divergent feature values for the same entity via null handling, window boundaries, time zones, rounding or type coercion.

Diagnoses `txn_count_24h` as a point-in-time-correctness problem: either training leaks future transactions (no strict as-of cutoff), inflating offline AUC, or the online counter is stale relative to training.

Diagnoses the ~30% missing `merchant_avg_ticket` as a train/serve distribution mismatch: training rarely saw the default/imputed value that a third of serving rows now get, concentrating error on those rows.

Proposes a concrete confirmation: feature logging plus recompute-and-diff (re-run the training pipeline for the same entity and as-of timestamp, compare vectors row-by-row) and/or per-feature PSI/KS between training and logged serving features.

Proposes eliminating the dual code path via a shared transformation layer or feature store (Feast/Tecton) with point-in-time-correct (as-of) training joins — ideally training on logged served features so distributions match by construction.

Adds prevention: consistent missing-value handling with an explicit missingness indicator and matching missing rate in training, plus continuous skew monitoring and shadow/canary comparison of served vs recomputed features before rollout.
common_pitfalls: Misdiagnoses the problem as data drift and prescribes retraining on recent data — but a flat gap present from hour one is skew (or a leaky eval); retraining does not close a code-path or leakage gap.
Blames model overfitting and reaches for regularization or more data, ignoring that the offline metric came from a held-out set and the gap is about feature computation, not variance.

Treats the 30% missing merchant_avg_ticket as merely 'needs imputation' without recognizing the train/serve distribution mismatch — imputing at serving to a value the training data almost never contained does not help.

Overlooks point-in-time correctness for txn_count_24h and proposes to 'just recompute the same feature online' without noticing the training pipeline may be leaking future data and inflating offline AUC.
Offers only monitoring/alerting (drift dashboards, PSI) as the fix — detection without correcting the dual code path or the leakage.
Suggests making serving match training (e.g., adding the future-window count online), which is causally impossible, instead of making training reflect the causal serving reality.
reference_answer:
Signature first. A gap that is present in the very first hour and stays flat — rather than sloping downward over weeks — is the fingerprint of training-serving skew and/or an optimistic offline evaluation, not data drift. Drift is temporal: the live distribution slowly moves away from training, so performance decays gradually. A constant day-one gap means the model is being fed different feature values in production than it learned from, or the offline number was never honest.

Mechanisms this setup invites:
- Two code paths. Features are built twice — nightly Spark/SQL over the warehouse for training, and online Python over Redis for serving. The two implementations inevitably diverge on null handling, 24h window boundaries, time zones, rounding and type coercion, so the same cardholder yields a different vector offline vs online.
- `txn_count_24h` — point-in-time correctness. If the Spark job counts over the whole day's table without a strict as-of cutoff, the training feature peeks at transactions that occurred after the scored one. That is leakage: offline AUC is inflated by information not causally available at serving. Conversely the online Redis counter can be stale (eventual consistency / TTL), so serving sees a weaker value than training.
- `merchant_avg_ticket` — missingness mismatch. 30% missing at serving but (near-)complete in the backfilled warehouse means training almost never saw the default/imputed value that a third of live rows now receive. The trees split on a region of feature space they never learned, and error concentrates on those rows.

Confirm the root cause. Turn on feature logging to capture the exact vectors served. Sample live scored transactions, re-run the training pipeline for the same entity and as-of timestamp, and diff row-by-row — non-trivial diffs localize the skew per feature. Complement with per-feature PSI / KS between the training set and the logged serving features; the skewed features light up. Re-evaluate offline with strictly point-in-time features to expose the leakage.

Fix and prevent. Kill the dual code path: put feature definitions in a shared transformation layer / feature store (Feast, Tecton) so offline and online compute identically, and generate training data with point-in-time-correct (as-of) joins. Better still, train on the logged served features so the training distribution equals the serving distribution by construction. Make missingness first-class — impute consistently in both paths, add an `is_missing` indicator, and ensure the training data carries the same missing rate rather than a backfilled complete table. Finally, stand up continuous skew monitoring (served-vs-recomputed feature diffs, PSI, per-feature missing-rate alerts) and shadow/canary new models before full rollout.
